note:
Thecla is an early Christian saint celebrated in the Acts of Paul and Thecla. In that narrative, she listens to Paul from a window in Iconium, rejects her arranged marriage, and bribes her way into prison to hear him teach.

The legend tells of a storm extinguishing her execution fire and a lioness defending her in the arena. She later baptizes herself, receives Paul’s commission to teach, and lives at Seleucia. These are episodes of the saint’s traditional life, not independently established biography.

note:
An Amesha Spenta: a beneficent immortal of Zoroastrian tradition. In its narrower use, the name denotes six divine beings associated with Ahura Mazda: Good Purpose, Best Righteousness, Desirable Dominion, Holy Devotion, Wholeness, and Immortality.

They are also linked to the care of cattle, fire, metals, earth, water, and plants. The tradition thus joins moral qualities to the protection of the material world. Broader uses of the name include other beneficent divinities.

note:
The Popol Vuh is the K’iche’ Maya account of creation, origins, and spiritual history, often called the Book of the Council or Book of the Community. Popol also denotes a woven mat, associated with communal gathering.

The Newberry manuscript was transcribed by Francisco Ximénez in Guatemala between 1700 and 1715. It presents K’iche’ in Latin letters beside a Spanish translation, preserving a work shaped by an older oral and written tradition.

note: A covered collecting case, usually metal, used by botanists to carry plant specimens.
short: A botanist’s case for plant specimens.

note: A short, large-bore cannon formerly used aboard ships for close-range fire.
short: A short naval cannon.

note: A water clock, measuring time by the gradual flow of water into or out of a vessel.
short: A water clock.

note: An enclosure in which living animals or plants are kept under conditions resembling their natural habitat.
short: An enclosure for living animals or plants.

note: A long, low couch, often without a back or arms.
short: A low couch or cushioned seat.

note: A sail set on the foremast or toward the forward part of a vessel.
short: A sail on the foremast or forward part of a ship.

note: A boy or young servant employed in a tavern to carry drinks and collect empty pots.
short: A tavern assistant who carries drinks.

note: A small boat carried by, or serving, a larger ship.
short: A small boat used with a larger vessel.

note: Yellow or yellowish.
short: Yellow or yellowish.

note: Involuntary imitation of another person’s movements or actions.
short: Involuntary imitation of another person’s movements.

note: A large, high-sided sailing ship used in European trade during the later Middle Ages and Renaissance.
short: A large, high-sided medieval sailing ship.

note: The traditional Christian office of prayer around three in the afternoon.
short: A traditional afternoon office of prayer.

note: A garden or enclosed ground laid out for enjoyment.
short: A pleasure garden or secluded garden area.

note: A sleepwalker.
short: A sleepwalker.

note: A servant who looks after horses at an inn or stable.
short: A stable worker who tends travelers’ horses.

note: A staff carried as an emblem of office, especially a bishop’s pastoral staff.
short: A staff or rod.

note: Stone cut into squared blocks with finished faces for building walls.
short: Squared stone cut for regular masonry.

note: A howler monkey.
short: A howler monkey.

note: Showy but worthless finery; things that look impressive without having real value.
short: Worthless showy objects or empty nonsense.

note: Persistently demanding attention or making requests in an intrusive way.
short: Persistently or annoyingly demanding.

note: A public entertainment with music and dancing, often a masquerade.
short: A public entertainment with music and dancing.

note: A large war galley propelled by both oars and sails and equipped with heavy guns.
short: A large galley powered by oars and sails.

note: A seal, emblem, or written sign, often one used in magic.
short: A seal, sign, or magical symbol.

note: The hard protective covering over an animal’s back, especially the upper shell of a turtle.
short: A hard protective shell.

note: The highest heaven, conceived as a realm of pure light or fire.
short: The highest heaven.

note: A tall, four-sided stone pillar that tapers toward a small pyramidal top.
short: A tall stone pillar tapering to a pyramid.

note: A worker of miracles or wonders.
short: A worker of wonders or miracles.

note: The mast aft of the mainmast on a vessel with three or more masts.
short: The mast behind the mainmast.

note: A large merchant ship, especially one carrying a rich cargo.
short: A large merchant ship or fleet.

note: An opening that lets air enter or escape; an air vent.
short: A breathing hole.

note: A masked or disguised performer in a traditional play or procession.
short: A masked performer or actor.

note: A mast behind the mainmast, or a fore-and-aft sail carried on that mast; also an adjective for its rigging.
short: A mast behind the mainmast, or its sail.

note: An upright stone slab bearing an inscription, carving, or commemorative design.
short: An upright stone slab or commemorative pillar.

note: The part of a sundial that casts the shadow used to indicate the time.
short: The shadow-casting part of a sundial.

note: Formed from small pieces fitted together, like a mosaic or tiled surface.
short: Formed into a mosaic or tiled pattern.

note: A drug or medicinal substance.
short: A drug or medicinal preparation.

note: The element mercury, also called quicksilver.
short: Mercury, the metallic element.

note: The central fortified tower or keep of a medieval castle.
short: The central stronghold of a castle.

note: The opening or arch that frames a theater stage and separates it from the audience.
short: The part of a stage before the curtain.

note: A slaughterhouse.
short: A slaughterhouse.

note: Clothing or dress; a covering garment.
short: Clothing or covering.

note: A banner suspended from a horizontal crossbar, often with a pointed or swallow-tailed lower edge.
short: A banner hanging from a crossbar.

note: Golden in color or ornamented with gold.
short: Golden or gilded.

note: A long shirt of mail armor, usually protecting the body and upper legs.
short: A shirt of mail armor.

note: In a low, quiet voice.
short: In a quiet or lowered voice.

note: A bell tower, particularly one standing separately beside a church.
short: A bell tower.

note: A member of a religious community who lives under a common rule, rather than as a solitary hermit.
short: A member of a communal religious order.

note: A divine maker or craftsman who shapes the material world, especially in Platonic and Gnostic thought.
short: A divine craftsman shaping the material world.

note: The innermost, secluded parts of a building, particularly a temple or sanctuary.
short: The innermost, secluded parts of a building.

note: A small Spanish riding horse.
short: A small Spanish riding horse.

note: A hermit, especially someone living alone for religious reasons.
short: A hermit.

note: A soft woven fabric with a fine ribbed texture, traditionally made of silk.
short: A softly ribbed woven fabric.

note: Black like ebony.
short: Black like ebony.

note: Sleep-inducing; as a noun, a substance that causes sleep.
short: Sleep-inducing.

note: Execution by drowning.
short: Execution by drowning.

note: A reddish or orange variety of zircon used as a gemstone.
short: A reddish or orange zircon gemstone.

note: Excrement; dung or other filth.
short: Excrement or filth.

note: A downward slope.
short: A downward slope.

note: A belt or girdle worn around the waist, especially with a robe.
short: A belt or girdle.

note: A mask or visor covering the face.
short: A mask or visor.

note: A person or spirit returned from the dead.
short: A person or spirit returned from the dead.

note: A serpent of classical legend with a head at each end, able to move in either direction.
short: A legendary serpent with a head at each end.

note: Thick, sticky, and slow-flowing.
short: Thick and sticky.

note: Packed closely together in rows or ranks.
short: Closely packed in rows.

note: A fetter or shackle, especially one fastening the ankles.
short: A fetter or shackle.

note: A deep green pigment, or its blue-green color.
short: A deep blue-green pigment or color.

note: A courier traveling on horseback.
short: A mounted courier.

note: Sodium, the metallic element whose chemical symbol is Na.
short: Sodium.

note: Foam or froth, especially on rough water.
short: Foam or froth.

note: A boatswain: the sailor responsible for a vessel’s rigging, deck equipment, and related work.
short: A boatswain, responsible for rigging and deck equipment.

note: An animal used to carry packs and supplies.
short: A pack animal.

note: One of the heavenly beings described in Isaiah 6, each with six wings, attending the divine throne.
short: A six-winged heavenly attendant in Isaiah.

note: A flask used in distillation, forming the lower vessel of an alembic.
short: The lower flask of a distilling apparatus.

note: The evening office of prayer in Christian tradition.
short: The evening office of Christian prayer.

note: The vertical distance between a ship’s waterline and the edge of its upper deck.
short: The height of a ship’s deck above its waterline.

note: A small writing desk with drawers or compartments for papers.
short: A small writing desk.

note: A food or drink made by cooking ground maize in liquid, to the consistency of porridge or thin gruel.
short: A maize-based drink or gruel.

note: An upright post or support, often part of a railing or barrier.
short: An upright post or support.

note: A rope or cable supporting a mast from behind.
short: A rope supporting a mast from behind.

note: A sitting of a court, especially a session held by judges traveling around a district.
short: A session of a court.

note: Describing a triangular sail hung from a long, slanting yard.
short: A triangular sail on a slanting yard.

note: A very large cask, especially one used for wine or beer.
short: A very large cask.

note: A lively, flirtatious maidservant character in comedy or opera, or the performer playing that part.
short: A lively maidservant character in comedy or opera.

note: The handle of an axe or other tool.
short: The handle of an axe or similar tool.

note: Flying; in heraldry, shown in flight with wings spread.
short: Flying; shown with wings spread.

note: A coat of arms or its formal heraldic description.
short: A coat of arms or its heraldic description.

note: To flash, sparkle, or give off small bursts of light.
short: To sparkle or flash.

note: Carved; an old form of the word.
short: Carved.

note: Made of marble or resembling it.
short: Made of or resembling marble.

note: A paid position requiring little or no work.
short: A paid position requiring little work.

note: An ancient Greek trumpet with a long, straight tube and a flared bell.
short: An ancient Greek straight trumpet.

note: A hand-operated mill for grinding grain, typically made from two stones.
short: A hand-operated grain mill.

note: A belt worn diagonally across the body to carry a sword or other equipment.
short: A diagonal belt carrying a sword.

note: The surrounding district or outskirts of a place.
short: The outskirts or surrounding district.

note: A stone coffin, often carved or decorated.
short: A stone coffin.

note: To cause stinging, itching, or raised welts on the skin.
short: To sting or cause itching welts.

note: An itemized list or memorandum of documents or accounts.
short: An itemized memorandum or list.

note: An extinct saber-toothed cat with exceptionally long upper canine teeth.
short: An extinct saber-toothed cat.

note: Merychippus: an extinct genus of American horses from the Miocene epoch.
short: Merychippus, an extinct American horse.

note: A large, extinct relative of the armadillo, protected by a rigid covering of bony plates.
short: A large, armored relative of the armadillo.

note: A large, extinct plant-eating mammal of Paleocene North America, with a small head and a heavy tail.
short: A heavy-bodied Paleocene plant-eating mammal.

note: A giant ground sloth of the extinct genus Megatherium.
short: An extinct giant ground sloth.

note: A metal headband that rises broadest above the forehead and narrows toward the temples, worn in ancient Greece.
short: An ancient Greek metal headband.

note: A guanaco: a wild, long-necked South American relative of the camel, with no hump and a thick coat.
short: A guanaco, a wild South American camel relative.

note: A small, malevolent, humanlike creature in Zulu folklore.
short: A small, malevolent being in Zulu folklore.

note: The Zulu word for a traditional healer, also borrowed into English as sangoma.
short: A traditional Zulu healer.

note: Possibly Saint Fara, a seventh-century Frankish abbess who founded the monastery of Faremoutiers.
short: Possibly Saint Fara, founder of Faremoutiers.

note: Possibly Saint Eata, a seventh-century Northumbrian monk, pupil of Aidan, abbot of Melrose, and bishop of Lindisfarne and Hexham.
short: Possibly Saint Eata, a Northumbrian bishop.

note: Possibly Saint Gurloës, also called Urlo, the first abbot of Sainte-Croix at Quimperlé in Brittany. He died in 1057.
short: Possibly Saint Gurloës, the abbot of Quimperlé.

note: Possibly Saint Ymar, a monk of Reculver in Kent remembered as a martyr killed by Danish raiders. His relics were venerated at Margate.
short: Possibly Saint Ymar, a monk of Reculver.

note: Possibly Saint Rudesind or Rosendo, a tenth-century Galician bishop and abbot who founded the monastery of Celanova.
short: Possibly Saint Rosendo, founder of Celanova.

note: Possibly Saint Hildegrim, an early medieval bishop of Châlons and abbot of Werden, the younger brother of the missionary Ludger.
short: Possibly Saint Hildegrim, bishop of Châlons.

note: Possibly Saint Agilus, a seventh-century Frankish monk and missionary who became the first abbot of Rebais, near Paris.
short: Possibly Saint Agilus, first abbot of Rebais.

note: Possibly Saint Trudo, a seventh-century religious founder whose monastery gave rise to Sint-Truiden in Belgium. He is traditionally called the Apostle of Hesbaye.
short: Possibly Saint Trudo, founder of Sint-Truiden.

note: Possibly Saint Pega, an Anglo-Saxon anchoress and sister of Saint Guthlac. She is associated with Peakirk, whose name means Pega’s church.
short: Possibly Saint Pega, an Anglo-Saxon anchoress.

note: Possibly Saint Anskar or Ansgar, a ninth-century missionary to Denmark and Sweden and archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen.
short: Possibly Saint Ansgar, a Scandinavian missionary.

note: Possibly Saint Declan, an Irish saint associated with the Déisi and Ardmore in County Waterford. His medieval Life places his mission before Patrick’s.
short: Possibly Saint Declan, associated with Ardmore.

note: Possibly Saint Odilo, an abbot of Cluny who established an annual commemoration of the faithful departed, an observance that developed into All Souls’ Day.
short: Possibly Saint Odilo, the abbot of Cluny.

note: Gjöll, the river on the road to Hel in Norse mythology. Its bridge, Gjallarbrú, is guarded by Móðguðr. Hermóðr crosses it when he journeys to the dead to seek Baldr.
short: Gjöll, the Norse river on the road to Hel.

note: A centaur and ferryman in Greek mythology. Heracles shot him after he attacked Deianira. Before dying, Nessus persuaded her that his blood was a love charm; the poisoned garment she later sent Heracles caused his death.
short: A centaur and ferryman of Greek mythology.

note: A bronze guardian of Crete in Greek mythology. He circled the island three times a day and hurled stones at approaching ships. A vein at his ankle was his vulnerable point.
short: The bronze guardian of Crete.

note: Zadkiel, an archangel associated with mercy and benevolence in Jewish and Christian angelology. The Hebrew name means “God is my righteousness.”
short: Zadkiel, an archangel associated with mercy.

note: A Roman deity who gives firmness to the bones of young children. The ancient writer Arnobius names her among the divinities assigned to specific tasks in human life.
short: A Roman deity who strengthens children’s bones.

note: The Vedic goddess of dawn. The Rigveda praises her as the daughter of the sky, arriving in light, awakening people and animals, and setting the day’s work in motion.
short: The Vedic goddess of dawn.

note: Hebrew for “foundation”; one of the ten sefirot in Kabbalah. It gathers and channels the divine influence of the preceding sefirot into Malkhut, the sefirah associated with the created world.
short: “Foundation,” one of the ten Kabbalistic sefirot.

note: Beri’ah, the “World of Creation” in Kabbalah. One of the four worlds, it lies below Atzilut, the World of Emanation. Here created beings are understood as distinct, though still dependent on the divine.

sources.label: Chabad: Beriya, the World of Creation

short: The Kabbalistic World of Creation.

note: A Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, meaning “destruction” or “place of destruction.” In the Book of Job it is paired with Sheol, the underworld.
short: A Hebrew name for destruction or the realm of the dead.

note: French for “moon,” from Latin luna.
short: French for moon.

note: Latin for “ice.”
short: Latin for ice.

note: A sword dancer dressed in an elaborate or fantastic costume.
short: A sword dancer in elaborate costume.

note: An Olympic spirit of Saturn in the sixteenth-century Arbatel, a treatise on ceremonial magic. The text assigns him powers of transformation and instruction in alchemy.
short: The Olympic spirit of Saturn in the Arbatel.

note: An Olympic spirit of Jupiter in the Arbatel. He is associated with dignities, riches, and the spirits of the air.
short: The Olympic spirit of Jupiter in the Arbatel.

note: An Olympic spirit of Mars in the Arbatel, associated with distinction in warfare.
short: The Olympic spirit of Mars in the Arbatel.

note: The first man in Zoroastrian creation tradition, also called Mashya or Mashye. In the Bundahishn, he and Mashyane emerge together from a plant.
short: Mashya, the first man in Zoroastrian tradition.

note: The first woman in Zoroastrian creation tradition, also called Mashyana or Mashyane. She and Mashya are the ancestral human pair in the Bundahishn.
short: Mashyane, the first woman in Zoroastrian tradition.

note: The female demon Jeh in the Bundahishn; Jahi is the corresponding Avestan form of the name. She rouses the destructive spirit Ahriman to attack creation.
short: Jeh, a female demon in Zoroastrian tradition.

note: A heavenly nymph in Vedic tradition. Rigveda 10.95 presents a dialogue between her and her mortal lover Pururavas.
short: A heavenly nymph in Vedic tradition.

note: The mortal lover of the heavenly nymph Urvasi. Their separation is the subject of a dialogue in Rigveda 10.95.
short: The mortal lover of Urvasi.

note: Verdandi, one of the three Norns of Norse mythology. With Urd and Skuld, she determines human lifespans; her name is associated with the present.
short: Verdandi, one of the three Norse Norns.

note: An amphibious, fish-shaped teacher in the Babylonian history attributed to Berossus. He comes from the sea to teach people writing, mathematics, agriculture, and the building of cities.
short: A fish-shaped Babylonian teacher of civilization.

note: The primeval mighty beings mentioned in Genesis 6:4, traditionally understood as giants. The passage places them among the renowned figures of the age before the Flood.
short: Primeval mighty beings mentioned in Genesis.

note: Droctoveus, a sixth-century monk and abbot of the Paris monastery later called Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A pupil of Germanus, he is traditionally said to have died around 580.
short: Droctoveus, a sixth-century abbot in Paris.

note: Ethor, a monk and priest of Chertsey Abbey in Surrey, venerated with Abbot Beocca among the community’s martyrs. Tradition places their deaths during Danish raids around 870.

sources.label: Catholic Church in Norway: the Chertsey martyrs

short: Ethor, a monk-priest and martyr of Chertsey.
Possibly Latin: edge; battle line.
note: Possibly Latin aciēs: the sharp edge or point of a blade. The same word extends to a line of battle or the keenness of sight. Its different senses share the idea of a directed, concentrated sharpness.

short: Possibly Greek: holy or sacred.
note: Possibly Greek hagía, the feminine of hágios, “holy” or “sacred.” Used before a woman’s name, Hagia is the Greek equivalent of Saint. Agia also occurs as a Latinized saint’s name, without selecting a unique historical woman.

short: A Quechua solar title: lord of day.
note: A Quechua solar title, usually understood as “lord of day.” Apu is a lord or powerful sacred being; punchaw means day or daylight. The two components give the title its solar meaning.

short: Possibly an extinct short-faced bear.
note: Possibly an extinct short-faced bear, such as Arctodus simus, a large bear of Ice Age North America.

sources.label: La Brea Tar Pits · mammal collections

short: Greek: silver.
note: Modern Greek asími (ασήμι): silver, the metal.

short: An insulting term: ill-born.
note: A disparaging formation meaning roughly “ill-born” or “of bad stock,” from Greek kakos, bad, and a root concerned with birth or origin. It expresses the speaker’s contempt, not a neutral biological classification.

short: Possibly Latin: a sword’s hilt.
note: Possibly Latin capulus, the handle or hilt of a sword. The same word can also mean a bier or coffin.

short: Possibly Saint Cyriaca of Rome.
note: Possibly Saint Cyriaca, a Roman widow remembered as a supporter of Saint Lawrence and a martyr. Her name is related to Greek kyriakós, “of the Lord.”

short: A crescent-shaped weapon.
note: A crescent-shaped weapon or blade. French demi-lune literally means “half-moon.” The same shape-word can also name a crescent-shaped work of fortification; it does not specify a weapon’s mechanism.

short: A cloak or outer jacket.
note: An outer garment, with two principal historical forms: a fitted, often braided military jacket of Hungarian origin, and a loose cloak or mantle with hanging or cape-like sleeves. The word alone does not require the close-fitting cavalry version.

short: A small measure of weight or volume.
note: A small measure, also spelled dram. Apothecaries used a drachm as a weight, while a fluid drachm measures liquid. Their values differ, and a liquid quantity should not be converted using the weight definition.

short: A high-ranking governor or prelate.
note: A high-ranking ruler or administrator. Byzantine exarchs governed distant territories with substantial civil and military powers; churches also use exarch for certain senior ecclesiastical officers. The title’s range is broader than either governor or bishop alone.

short: Triumphantly joyful.
note: Rejoicing intensely or triumphantly; from Latin exsultare, to leap up or rejoice.

short: Possibly the painter Nicolai Fechin.
note: Possibly Nicolai Fechin (1881–1955), the Russian-born painter celebrated for vigorous portraits and richly worked surfaces. He trained under Ilya Repin, later settled in Taos, New Mexico, and also carved elaborate woodwork. His portraits often combine precise faces with freer, highly textured surroundings.

short: Possibly Latin fuligo: soot.
note: Possibly Latin fuligo, soot. The related English adjective fuliginous means sooty or dark and smoky.

short: A sword or long-bladed weapon.
note: An old word for a sword, also used for a pole weapon with a long cutting blade. Historical usage is not confined to the modern museum sense of a single-edged blade mounted on a shaft.

short: An earth spirit; a wizened little figure.
note: In Renaissance accounts of elemental spirits, a gnome belongs to the earth and may guard underground treasure. The word later became a figurative description of a small, wizened person. That figurative use does not assert that someone is literally a supernatural creature.

short: Latin: to enter or begin.
note: Latin inīre, the infinitive of ineo: to enter, begin, undertake, or form an agreement.

short: Possibly Máel Ruba of Applecross.
note: Possibly Máel Ruba, the Irish-born founder of Applecross in western Scotland in 673. Malrubius is a recorded Latinized form of his name. Later traditions present him as a martyr killed by Norse raiders, but their places and dates are not consistent with the early annalistic record.

short: Possibly Saint Maxellende of Caudry.
note: Possibly Saint Maxellende of Caudry, a seventh-century martyr. In her legend, she refuses an arranged marriage after choosing a religious life; her rejected suitor kills her and becomes blind. His sight returns after repentance. She is traditionally invoked for eye ailments.

short: Possibly a Christian ascetic of Bithynia.
note: Possibly Nicarete, an early Christian ascetic from Bithynia and supporter of John Chrysostom. The historian Sozomen describes her loss of wealth, economical household, and preparation of remedies for poor patients. She declined prominent religious responsibilities, preferring a less public life.

short: Possibly an early Egyptian hermit.
note: Possibly Palaemon, the Egyptian hermit who instructed Saint Pachomius in ascetic life. Pachomius later established organized monastic communities; Palaemon represents the older discipline of the solitary desert monk.

short: Possibly Saint Roch, a pilgrim and healer.
note: Possibly Saint Roch, the French pilgrim traditionally invoked against plague. His legend describes his care for sick people in Italy, his own illness, and a dog bringing him bread. French roche also means rock.

short: Possibly Saint Severian of Scythopolis.
note: Possibly Saint Severian, the fifth-century bishop of Scythopolis killed during the disputes following the Council of Chalcedon. Severianus is a Roman name derived from Severus, stern or serious.

short: An air spirit; a slender, graceful figure.
note: A spirit of the air in the elemental system associated with Paracelsus. Sylphs later became familiar figures in poetry and ballet, and the word also describes a slender, graceful person. The figurative sense need not imply a literal spirit.

short: Latin: it is the end or boundary.
note: Latin: it is the end, or this is the boundary. Terminus means a limit, boundary, or end; est means is. Terminus was also the Roman god of boundary markers.

short: The extinct Tasmanian tiger.
note: The thylacine, also called the Tasmanian tiger or Tasmanian wolf: an extinct, dog-shaped carnivorous marsupial. Despite those common names, it was neither a cat nor a wolf. Thylacinus comes from a Greek word for a sack or pouch.

short: A wall panel or its decorative mirror.
note: A section of wall between openings, or a decorative panel or mirror associated with that space. In furniture and interior decoration, a trumeau often has a mirror below an ornamental or painted upper panel. It need not refer to a structural pier.

short: A Roman name associated with strength.
note: The feminine form of the Roman family name Valerius, traditionally connected with Latin valere, “to be strong” or “to be well.” The same root survives in words concerned with vigor and worth.

short: Compare zoanthropy: belief in being an animal.
note: Related to zoanthropy, a historical term for the delusion that one has become an animal. The roots are Greek zōion, animal, and anthrōpos, human being.

short: An opening beneath a projecting battlement.
note: An opening in the floor of a projecting battlement, allowing defenders to act directly against an attacker below the wall. In the plural, the word can refer to the projecting defensive arrangement as a whole.

short: Originating in another land or region.
note: Originating in a different land or region; foreign to the place under discussion. The formation joins Greek heteros, other, with chthon, earth or land. It is the opposite kind of idea to autochthonous, native to the same soil.

short: A horseman of the South American plains.
note: An inhabitant of the llanos, the broad plains of Venezuela and Colombia, especially a cattle-herding horseman. Spanish llano means a plain or level tract of land.

short: A low sighing or moaning sound.
note: A low, continuous sighing, rushing, or moaning sound, especially the sound of wind among trees or through a narrow opening. The verb means to make that sound.

short: Shining with brilliant light.
note: Brightly shining or radiant, especially with reflected or splendid light. It is a more emphatic word than merely visible or pale.

short: Latin: radiance or a heavenly light.
note: Latin iubar: radiance, a beam of light, or a bright heavenly body, especially the sun. The spelling jubar is a later way of writing the same Latin word.

short: Possibly armiger: a bearer of arms.
note: Possibly a feminine formation from armiger, a bearer of arms or someone entitled to heraldic arms. Latin armiger means arms-bearer.

short: Dry and withered.
note: Dry, withered, or stripped of freshness, especially of vegetation. A literary description of leaves or land, rather than a statement about temperature alone.

short: A boy or young man kept for sexual use.
note: A historical, derogatory term for a boy or young man kept for sexual use by an older man. It descends from Latin Catamitus, the Roman form of Ganymede’s name. The term belongs to the history of sexual exploitation, not to a neutral description of an orientation.

short: A stand or frame for a coffin.
note: A frame or stand on which a dead body or coffin is carried or displayed. The word is related to bear in the sense of carrying a weight.

short: A railing supported by small pillars.
note: A row of small pillars, called balusters, supporting a rail. The term names the whole barrier along a stair, balcony, or terrace, rather than one of its supports.

short: A set of bells played as an instrument.
note: A set of tuned bells that can sound a melody, usually housed in a tower and played from a keyboard. The word can also refer to the tune or performance.

short: A compact, memorable saying.
note: A brief, pointed saying that expresses a general observation or practical truth. It is close to an aphorism or maxim; the spelling apophthegm is also used.

short: A complete array or splendid display.
note: A full array, often splendid or impressive. The word originally referred to a complete suit of armor, from Greek panoplia, “all the armor,” and still carries that sense of completeness.

short: A loyal, unquestioning subordinate.
note: A follower who carries out orders without question or scruple. The name comes from the Myrmidons, the warriors led by Achilles in Greek epic.

short: A vivid scarlet-red color.
note: A bright scarlet red. The pigment traditionally called vermilion is mercuric sulfide, while the color word can be used without specifying the material that produces it.

short: A low barrier controlling water or fish.
note: A low dam or barrier across flowing water, used to divert or regulate it. A weir can also be a fence-like structure arranged to trap fish.

short: A small lake, especially in the hills.
note: A small lake, especially one in mountainous country. The word came into English from Old Norse and remains common in the place-names of northern Britain.

short: Worn or haggard in appearance.
note: Looking worn down, exhausted, or damaged, especially in the face. It describes an appearance rather than a particular illness.

short: An old word meaning shadowless.
note: An inhabitant of a tropical region where the overhead sun can leave no shadow at noon; from Greek words for without and shadow.

short: An old word for north.
note: The north or northern regions. Latin septentriones names seven northern stars, literally seven plowing oxen.

short: French: a female pilgrim; also a cape.
note: French pèlerine means a female pilgrim. In English, pelerine denotes a cape or mantle covering the shoulders.

short: Possibly the mythical lover of Galatea.
note: Possibly Acis, the shepherd loved by Galatea in classical myth. Killed by the jealous Polyphemus, he was transformed into a river.

short: Possibly a Messenian hero.
note: Possibly Idas, a hero of Greek myth, son of Aphareus and brother of Lynceus, who carried off Marpessa in a winged chariot.

short: An astrological giver of life.
note: In traditional astrology, a planet or point treated as the giver of life in a natal chart. The Greek word means a releaser.

short: Latin: bonds or fetters.
note: Latin vincula, plural of vinculum: bonds, chains, or fetters; also imprisonment.

short: Latin: woodland or forest pasture.
note: Latin saltus can mean woodland, forested upland, or uncultivated pasture.

short: Possibly Blessed Jolenta of Poland.
note: Possibly Blessed Jolenta of Poland, a Hungarian princess who became a Poor Clare and abbess after her husband’s death.

short: Possibly Saint Ultan of Ardbraccan.
note: Possibly Saint Ultan of Ardbraccan, an Irish abbot, bishop, and writer remembered for caring for poor children.

short: Possibly the bishop of Sardis.
note: Possibly Melito, the second-century bishop of Sardis and an early Christian writer.

short: Possibly a Roman martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Daria, a Roman martyr venerated with Saint Chrysanthus; their burial place was on the Via Salaria.

short: Possibly Latin “bearded,” recalling Fortuna Barbata.
note: Possibly Latin barbatus, “bearded.” In The City of God, Augustine discusses Fortuna Barbata, the deity who gives young men their beards, and proposes Barbatus as a masculine name for her.

sources.label: Augustine · The City of God, Book IV

short: Possibly Jonah, the biblical prophet.
note: Possibly Jonah, also called Jonas, the biblical prophet who fled the command to preach at Nineveh and was swallowed by a great fish.

short: Possibly Oslo’s patron saint.
note: Possibly Saint Hallvard, the eleventh-century Norwegian martyr and patron saint of Oslo.

short: Possibly the Persian martyr Kazdoa.
note: Possibly Kazdoa, also called Kasdoe, a Persian martyr commemorated with Dadas and Gabdelas in Christian tradition.

short: Possibly Saint Foila of Killeely.
note: Possibly Saint Foila, the Irish saint credited with founding Killeely Church in County Galway. Her tomb became a place of pilgrimage.

short: Possibly a Cornish saint.
note: Possibly Saint Morwenna, the local saint commemorated in the dedication of the parish church at Morwenstow, Cornwall.

short: Possibly Saint Hadelin of Celles.
note: Possibly Saint Hadelin, the seventh-century religious founder associated with Celles in present-day Belgium.

short: Latin: a Thracian.
note: Latin Thrax means a Thracian, a person from ancient Thrace in southeastern Europe.

short: Possibly Greek: iron.
note: Possibly Greek sidēros, iron, also the source of the combining form sidero- in English.

short: Possibly Saint Abdiesus, a Persian Christian martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Abdiesus, also called Hebedjesus. A deacon remembered among the Christians killed during Shapur II’s persecution in fourth-century Persia.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Herena, an African martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Herena. Named with Donatus, Justus, and other African martyrs traditionally associated with the persecution of Decius.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Guasacht, an early Irish bishop.
note: Possibly Saint Guasacht of Granard. Irish tradition makes him a son of Patrick’s former enslaver and a convert whom Patrick appointed bishop at Granard.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Pia, an early African martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Pia. One of a group of African Christians remembered with Paul and Gerontius. Little biographical information survives.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Zama, an early bishop of Bologna.
note: Possibly Saint Zama, also called Zamas. Traditionally the first recorded bishop of Bologna, assigned to the third century.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Becan, an early Irish monastic name.
note: Possibly one of the early Irish saints named Becan. One founded a monastery at Kilbeggan; another is remembered as a hermit near Cork. Both belong to sixth-century Irish religious tradition.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Barrog, the hermit associated with Barry Island.
note: Possibly Saint Barrog, also called Barruc or Barnoch. A Welsh hermit traditionally linked to Saint Cadoc and to Barry Island off Glamorgan.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Cybi, associated with Holyhead.
note: Possibly Saint Cybi, also called Cuby or Cyby. An early British church founder whose foundations are remembered in Cornwall and Wales, especially the monastery at Holyhead.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Piaton, missionary and martyr at Tournai.
note: Possibly Saint Piaton, or Piat. An early Christian missionary traditionally associated with Tournai and Chartres, commemorated as a martyr of the Roman persecutions.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Llibio, remembered in Anglesey.
note: Possibly Saint Llibio, also spelled Libio. An early Welsh saint whose name survives in Llanllibio on Anglesey.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Ouen, seventh-century bishop of Rouen.
note: Possibly Saint Ouen, also called Audoenus or Audoin. A Frankish court official who became bishop of Rouen and a close associate of Saint Eligius.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Eskil, a missionary to Sweden.
note: Possibly Saint Eskil. A missionary bishop associated with Saint Sigfrid, remembered as a martyr in eleventh-century Sweden.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Lomer, a sixth-century French abbot.
note: Possibly Saint Lomer, also called Launomar or Laudomarus. An abbot associated with the region of Chartres, remembered in monastic tradition for miracles.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Eusebia, a martyr remembered at Bergamo.
note: Possibly Saint Eusebia of Bergamo. A Christian martyr of Lombard tradition, associated with Saint Domnio and the persecutions under Maximian.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Severa, an abbess at Trier.
note: Possibly Saint Severa of Trier. Traditionally the sister of Bishop Modoald and abbess of a convent founded by him at Trier.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Thaïs, an Egyptian penitent.
note: Possibly Saint Thaïs of Egyptian monastic legend. Tradition describes a courtesan converted by Paphnutius who spent years in seclusion and penitence.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Merinus or Merryn, an Irish monastic saint.
note: Possibly Saint Merinus, also called Merryn or Meadhran. Remembered as a disciple of Comgall of Bangor and venerated in Ireland and Scotland. Several similar saint names have become entangled in later tradition.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Stachys, named in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.
note: Possibly Saint Stachys. Paul sends greetings to Stachys in Romans 16:9. Later church tradition makes him the first bishop of Byzantium.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Jader, an African bishop sent to the mines.
note: Possibly Saint Jader. Named among the African bishops condemned to forced labor during the persecution of Valerian. Cyprian wrote a letter of encouragement to this group.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Chuniald, a companion of Rupert of Salzburg.
note: Possibly Saint Chuniald. An early medieval missionary associated with Rupert’s work in southern Germany and the Salzburg region.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Jurmin, an East Anglian prince.
note: Possibly Saint Jurmin. An early English prince venerated as a saint; his relics were kept at Bury St Edmunds. The details of his life are uncertain.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Nennoc, an abbess of Brittany.
note: Possibly Saint Nennoc, also called Ninnoc. A saint of British origin traditionally credited with founding and governing religious communities in Armorica, now Brittany.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Modan, a Scottish monastic saint.
note: Possibly Saint Modan. A Scottish abbot associated with preaching around Stirling and Falkirk and with a later hermit’s life near Dumbarton.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Leocadia, a martyr of Toledo.
note: Possibly Saint Leocadia of Toledo. A Spanish martyr traditionally dated to Diocletian’s persecution, honored as a patron saint of Toledo.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Marcellina, sister of Ambrose of Milan.
note: Possibly Saint Marcellina. A fourth-century consecrated virgin. Her brother Ambrose addressed letters and religious writings to her.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Talarican, a missionary bishop in Scotland.
note: Possibly Saint Talarican, also called Tarkin. A saint associated especially with Aberdeenshire. Traditions about his origins and dates differ.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Werenfrid, a missionary among the Frisians.
note: Possibly Saint Werenfrid. An English missionary associated with Willibrord’s work in the Netherlands and with the district around Arnhem.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Manahen, a prophet and teacher at Antioch.
note: Possibly Manahen, or Manaen, of the Acts of the Apostles. Acts 13:1 names him among the church’s prophets and teachers and says he was brought up with Herod the tetrarch.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Barbea, a martyr of Edessa.
note: Possibly Saint Barbea. A Christian woman of Syrian tradition, commemorated as a martyr at Edessa.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Ibar, an early Irish missionary.
note: Possibly Saint Ibar, also called Iberius. A saint associated with evangelizing Leinster and Meath. His relationship to Patrick varies among the surviving traditions.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Lactan, an Irish monastic founder.
note: Possibly Saint Lactan, also called Lachtin or Lactinus. An Irish abbot associated with Comgall of Bangor and the monastery at Freshford in County Kilkenny.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Loman, bishop of Trim.
note: Possibly Saint Loman of Trim. Traditionally an early bishop of Trim in County Meath and a kinsman of Patrick.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Maruthas, a bishop active in Persian Christianity.
note: Possibly Saint Maruthas. A Mesopotamian bishop and church diplomat remembered for aiding Christians in Persia and restoring churches after persecution.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Nilammon, an Egyptian recluse.
note: Possibly Saint Nilammon. In his traditional life he refuses election as bishop and dies while praying before the appointment can be imposed on him.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Sebald, a hermit honored at Nuremberg.
note: Possibly Saint Sebald, or Sebaldus. A missionary hermit whose shrine is in the Nuremberg church that bears his name. His biography is largely legendary.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Solange, a French shepherdess and martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Solange of Bourges. A shepherdess in the region of Bourges. Her legend says she was killed after resisting a nobleman’s sexual assault.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Cinnia, an Irish princess and nun.
note: Possibly Saint Cinnia. Irish tradition makes her a princess of Ulster converted by Patrick who entered a religious community.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Ceallach, an early bishop of Killala.
note: Possibly Saint Ceallach, also called Kellach. A saint associated with the monastery of Clonmacnoise, the bishopric of Killala, and a later life as a hermit.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Abban, the name of early Irish abbots.
note: Possibly one of the Irish saints called Abban. Irish tradition remembers both an Abban associated with Kill-Abban in Leinster and another credited with founding monasteries in southern Ireland.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Hadrian, a soldier-martyr of Nicomedia.
note: Possibly Saint Hadrian, also called Adrian, of Nicomedia. Christian tradition describes an imperial officer who converted after witnessing the endurance of prisoners and was himself tortured and executed.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Fausta, a young martyr of Cyzicus.
note: Possibly Saint Fausta of Cyzicus. A girl commemorated in Christian tradition with Evilasius, who is said to have converted after seeing her endure torture.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Eusignius, a veteran soldier and martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Eusignius of Antioch. Tradition describes a very old soldier executed under Julian after refusing pagan worship.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Epicharis, an early Christian martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Epicharis. Commemorated as a woman killed during Diocletian’s persecution; traditions disagree over whether the location was Rome or Constantinople.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Decuman, a Welsh hermit in Somerset.
note: Possibly Saint Decuman. A saint associated with Watchet in Somerset, traditionally said to have been murdered while living as a hermit.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Bregwin, an archbishop of Canterbury.
note: Possibly Saint Bregwin. An eighth-century archbishop of Canterbury whose life was later written by the historian Eadmer.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Winnoc, an abbot honored in Flanders.
note: Possibly Saint Winnoc, also spelled Winoc. An early medieval abbot associated with Saint Bertin’s community near Saint-Omer.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Abundantius, a deacon-martyr of Rome.
note: Possibly Saint Abundantius. Traditionally commemorated with the priest Abundius and the Christians Marcian and John as victims of Roman persecution.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Chad, a seventh-century English bishop.
note: Possibly Saint Chad, also called Ceadda. A Northumbrian churchman who became bishop of the Mercians and established his episcopal seat at Lichfield.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Gildas, author of On the Ruin of Britain.
note: Possibly Saint Gildas the Wise. A sixth-century British cleric whose Latin work rebukes rulers and clergy and describes the troubles of post-Roman Britain.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Odo, a reforming abbot of Cluny.
note: Possibly Saint Odo of Cluny. A tenth-century Benedictine abbot who helped spread the Cluniac movement for reform of monastic life.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Jovinian, a Christian lector and martyr.
note: Possibly Saint Jovinian of Auxerre. A missionary companion of Peregrinus of Auxerre, remembered for scriptural learning and martyrdom in Gaul.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Pope Hormisdas, who reconciled Rome and Constantinople.
note: Possibly Pope Saint Hormisdas. Pope from 514 to 523, remembered for ending the Acacian schism between the churches of Rome and Constantinople.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Mamas, a martyr honored in Cappadocia.
note: Possibly Saint Mamas, also called Mammas. An early Christian martyr associated with Caesarea in Cappadocia. His traditional lives differ substantially.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Phocas, a bishop-martyr of Sinope.
note: Possibly Saint Phocas of Sinope. A saint traditionally identified as a bishop of Sinope on the Black Sea, executed during the reign of Trajan.

sources.label: Monks of Ramsgate · The Book of Saints (1921)

short: Possibly Saint Mannea, remembered with her family.
note: Possibly Saint Mannea, a Christian martyr commemorated with her husband Marcellinus and their children.

short: Possibly Saint Thea, a martyr of Gaza.
note: Possibly Saint Thea, commemorated with Meuris as a Christian martyr of Gaza. The surviving traditions about these two women are uncertain.

sources.label: French Bishops’ Conference · Thea and Meuris

short: Possibly a Germanic name formed from “battle” and “wolf.”
note: Possibly the medieval name Gundulf, formed from Germanic elements meaning “battle” and “wolf.” It was borne by several early medieval saints.

short: Possibly Saint Hermeland, also known as Herbland.
note: Possibly Saint Hermeland, also called Herbland, a Benedictine abbot who founded a monastery on the island of Indre near Nantes. His name survives in Saint-Erblon.

sources.label: Pays de la Loire heritage inventory · Saint Hermeland

short: Possibly Saint Domnina of Syria, a fifth-century ascetic.
note: Possibly Saint Domnina the Younger of Syria, an ascetic described by Theodoret of Cyrrhus. She lived in a small shelter and devoted herself to prayer, austerity, and care for others.

sources.label: Orthodox Church in America · Domnina of Syria

short: Possibly Saint Ava, a nun of Denain.
note: Possibly Saint Ava, a ninth-century saint venerated at Denain in northern France. Tradition says she entered the monastery after being healed of blindness.

short: Possibly Saint Hunna, remembered for washing for the poor.
note: Possibly Saint Hunna, an Alsatian noblewoman remembered for serving poor neighbors, especially by washing their clothes. She is a patron saint of laundresses.

short: Possibly Saint Racho, a bishop of Autun.
note: Possibly Saint Racho, also called Ragnobert, a seventh-century bishop of Autun in France.

short: Possibly Budoc, a Breton saint whose name survives as Beuzec.
note: Possibly Saint Budoc, an early Breton saint. The Breton place-name Beuzec preserves his name; the church at Beuzec-Cap-Sizun is dedicated to him.

sources.label: Fondation du patrimoine · Saint-Budoc at Beuzec

short: Possibly Saint Mamillian, a bishop of Palermo.
note: Possibly Saint Mamillian, or Mamiliano, an early bishop of Palermo. Tradition associates him with exile in Tuscany during the Vandal period.

short: Possibly Mesrop Mashtots, creator of the Armenian alphabet.
note: Possibly Saint Mesrop Mashtots, a fifth-century Armenian monk who devised the Armenian alphabet around 405. His work enabled a major movement of translation and literary production in Armenian.

short: Possibly Saint Catherine of Alexandria, associated with the wheel.
note: Possibly Saint Catherine of Alexandria, a Christian martyr of legend. A spiked wheel and a sword are her familiar attributes, recalling the torture and execution in her traditional life.

sources.label: Metropolitan Museum of Art · Catherine of Alexandria

short: Possibly Hermas, author of The Shepherd.
note: Possibly Hermas, the early Christian author traditionally credited with The Shepherd, a work of visions, commands, and allegorical parables. This author is generally distinguished from the Hermas named in Romans 16:14.

sources.label: The Shepherd of Hermas · translated text

short: Possibly from Latin famulus: a servant or attendant.
note: Possibly related to Latin famulus, “servant” or “slave,” also the source of English famulus, a close attendant or assistant.

short: Possibly Latin: “of the servants.”
note: Possibly Latin famulorum, “of the servants,” the genitive plural of famulus, a servant or slave.

short: Possibly from Latin gurgustium: a hut or hovel.
note: Possibly from Latin gurgustium, a small hut, hovel, or dark cramped dwelling. Gurgustii is a genitive form, “of a hovel.”

short: Possibly Latin vici: villages or neighborhoods.
note: Possibly Latin vici, the plural of vicus, a village or a neighborhood of a town.

short: Possibly from Latin litus: a shore or beach.
note: Possibly from Latin litus, a seashore, beach, or landing place.

short: Possibly Latin os: a mouth or opening.
note: Possibly Latin os, “mouth,” extended to an opening or entrance.

short: Possibly Latin: “of a river.”
note: Possibly Latin fluminis, “of a river” or “of a stream,” from flumen.

short: Possibly Latin noctua: an owl.
note: Possibly Latin noctua, an owl, particularly a night owl; the bird was associated with Minerva.

short: Possibly Latin quiesco: “I rest” or “I am still.”
note: Possibly Latin quiesco, “I rest,” “I sleep,” or “I keep still.”

short: Possibly Latin pestis: plague, ruin, or destruction.
note: Possibly Latin pestis, a plague or deadly disease; more broadly, a destructive calamity or a source of ruin.

short: Possibly Latin carina: a ship’s keel.
note: Possibly Latin carina, the keel of a ship, also used poetically for the whole vessel.

short: Possibly Latin silva: a wood or forest.
note: Possibly Latin silva, a wood, forest, or woodland.

short: Possibly Latin miles: a soldier.
note: Possibly Latin miles, a soldier; in medieval Latin the word can also mean a knight.

short: Possibly related to the Latin ancestor of “damsel.”
note: Possibly related to domnicella, a reconstructed popular Latin word for a young woman or maiden, behind French demoiselle and English damsel.

short: Possibly Avernus, the lake associated with an entrance to the underworld.
note: Possibly Avernus, a volcanic lake near ancient Cumae in Italy. In Virgil’s Aeneid it is an entrance to the underworld, and its name is explained through a tradition that birds could not fly safely above it.

short: Possibly Abaia, a great magical eel in Melanesian tradition.
note: Possibly Abaia, a magical eel in a Melanesian flood tale. When people catch fish from its lake, it sends a deluge in retaliation.

short: Possibly the Simurgh, a mythical bird of Iranian tradition.
note: Possibly the Simurgh, or Sēnmurw, the great mythical bird of Iranian tradition. In Persian epic the bird protects Zal and later aids his son Rostam.

short: Possibly Oreithyia, the Athenian princess carried off by the north wind.
note: Possibly Oreithyia, or Orithyia, daughter of the Athenian king Erechtheus. Greek myth tells how Boreas, the north wind, carried her away to become his wife.

short: Possibly Alcyone, transformed with Ceyx into a sea bird.
note: Possibly Alcyone, or Halcyone, whose grief for her shipwrecked husband Ceyx ends with both transformed into birds in Ovid’s Metamorphoses. Their nesting season is associated with the calm “halcyon days.”

short: Possibly Keryx, the herald associated with the Eleusinian mysteries.
note: Possibly Keryx, or Ceryx, a legendary herald and ancestor of the Athenian priestly family of the Kerykes. One tradition makes him a son of Hermes.

sources.label: Theoi · Hermes’ family and classical passages

short: Possibly Dis, the Roman god of the underworld.
note: Possibly Dis, or Dis Pater, a Roman name for the ruler of the underworld, identified with Pluto and the Greek Hades.

short: Possibly Skuld, one of the Norse Norns.
note: Possibly Skuld, one of the three Norns who determine human lifespans in Norse myth. The Prose Edda also numbers her among the Valkyries who choose the slain.

short: Possibly Cephissus, a Greek river and river-god.
note: Possibly Cephissus, or Kephisos, the name of several Greek rivers and their personified river-gods, including the river of Phocis and Boeotia.

short: Unfading; also a reddish-purple color.
note: Unfading or everlasting; also the reddish-purple color called amaranth. The word is related to Greek amarantos, unfading.

short: A flowing robe or light shift.
note: An old garment name covering a flowing Renaissance gown, a light shift, or a long outer robe.

short: A regional name for the Canada lynx.
note: A New England name for the Canada lynx, adapted from Canadian French loup-cervier.

short: A penitential garment of the Inquisition.
note: A garment imposed on penitents and condemned people by the Spanish Inquisition, marked with crosses or images of flames and devils.

short: A ribbed silk fabric.
note: A silk fabric woven with a pronounced corded or ribbed texture; also a garment made from it.

short: A sweet, flavored cordial.
note: A sweetened spirit flavored with ingredients such as rose petals, orange blossoms, cinnamon, or cloves.

short: A faint glow opposite the Sun.
note: A faint patch of light in the night sky opposite the Sun, produced by sunlight scattered back by interplanetary dust. German Gegenschein means counterglow.

short: A chorus leader.
note: The leader of a chorus; more generally, the leading figure in a movement or school of thought. From Greek koryphaios, chief or foremost.

short: A poem retracting an earlier poem.
note: A poem or song that withdraws a statement made in an earlier work; more broadly, a formal recantation.

short: A battle banner or rallying symbol.
note: Originally the red banner associated with Saint Denis and carried by medieval French kings in battle; later, any banner or ideal that inspires devotion.

short: An ancient 3,600-year period; also an eclipse cycle.
note: In ancient Babylonian chronology, a period of 3,600 years. In modern astronomy, a cycle of about 6,585.3 days, or eighteen years, after which similar eclipses recur.

sources.label: Verbrugghe and Wickersham · Berossos and Manetho

short: The entrance area of a church.
note: A vestibule or porch at the entrance to a church, leading into its main interior.

short: A junior heraldic officer.
note: An officer of arms below the rank of herald, performing similar ceremonial and heraldic duties. The word also means a follower or attendant.

short: A pilgrim to the Holy Land.
note: A pilgrim who has visited the Holy Land, traditionally wearing crossed palm leaves as a sign of the journey.

short: Of Paphos; an old term for a sex worker.
note: Belonging to Paphos in Cyprus. In older English, a paphian can mean a female sex worker, and the adjective can describe illicit love.

short: A mountain nymph.
note: A nymph of hills or mountains in Greek mythology; the name comes from Greek oros, mountain.

short: Church property supporting a religious household.
note: Relating to a table; historically also applied to a church or property whose revenues maintained a bishop’s table or household. From Latin mensa, table.

short: A Parisian seamstress or shopgirl.
note: A traditional French name for a young Parisian seamstress or shop assistant.

short: An azure-blue phosphate mineral.
note: A blue mineral containing aluminum, magnesium, iron, and phosphate. Its name recalls the color of lapis lazuli.

short: Fine, downy body hair.
note: A soft, downy covering of hair, especially the hair of a mammalian fetus. Latin lanugo means down and is related to lana, wool.

short: A helmet scarf or decorative valance.
note: A cloth draped over a helmet; also a short decorative hanging along the top of a window or the edge of a shelf.

short: A glasslike form of opal.
note: A usually colorless variety of opal with a glasslike appearance, sometimes cloudy or whitish.

short: Irregular or unconventional.
note: Departing from customary forms or rules. In grammar, a heteroclite is a word with irregular inflection.

short: The six days of Creation.
note: The six days of Creation in Genesis; from Greek words meaning six and day.

short: A yellow pigment from tree resin.
note: A resin obtained from Garcinia trees of Southeast Asia and used as a yellow pigment; also the strong yellow color itself.

short: A great magician.
note: An eminent magician or enchanter; from Greek elements meaning chief and magus.

short: A dawn song or poem.
note: A poem or musical piece associated with daybreak, particularly a song of lovers separating at dawn.

short: An ominous spectral dog or goblin.
note: A ghost or goblin in English folklore, often appearing as a large dog and regarded as an omen of misfortune.

short: The mineral of emerald and aquamarine.
note: A hard mineral composed of beryllium aluminum silicate. Its colored varieties include emerald, aquamarine, heliodor, and morganite.

short: Shimmering like a cat’s eye.
note: Showing a shifting, luminous band as the surface turns, especially in a gemstone; from French chatoyer, to shine like a cat’s eyes.

short: Cordovan leather.
note: An old English name for cordovan leather, with a word history running through French to Spanish cordobán.

short: Latin: a leader or commander.
note: Latin dux means leader. In the later Roman Empire it became a title for a provincial military commander.

short: A thick, shaggy woolen cloth.
note: A heavy woolen fabric with a rough surface, used for protective outer clothing; also a garment made from it.

short: A German mercenary foot soldier.
note: A German infantry mercenary of the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries; from German Landsknecht. The word also names an old card game.

short: A vessel displaying the Eucharist.
note: A vessel designed to display the consecrated Eucharistic host for veneration. The name is related to Latin monstrare, to show.

short: Glowing or visible at night.
note: Shining or becoming visible at night; also used for organisms that produce light.

short: People whose shadows turn all around them.
note: An old geographical term, also spelled periscii, for people within a polar circle whose shadows sweep around them during the continuous daylight of summer.

short: Mandrake, a plant of magical folklore.
note: Mandrake: a Mediterranean plant of the nightshade family whose forked root can resemble a human figure and was traditionally credited with magical powers.

short: Open to the sky.
note: Hypaethral: having a central space open to the sky, especially a temple with an uncovered interior.

short: Possibly burgonet, a Renaissance helmet.
note: Possibly burgonet, a close-fitting helmet with cheek guards used in the sixteenth century.

short: A short medieval coat of mail.
note: A coat of mail generally shorter than a hauberk; also spelled habergeon.

short: Possibly Greek chrysos: gold.
note: Possibly Greek chrysos (χρυσός), gold, also used collectively for objects made from gold.

short: Latin: copper, bronze, or money.
note: Latin aes means copper or bronze and, by extension, objects made from those metals, including money.

sources.label: Lewis and Short Latin dictionary · Perseus

short: Possibly dimachae: cavalry fighting on foot.
note: Possibly dimachae, Macedonian troops trained to fight both on horseback and as infantry.

sources.label: Anthony Rich · Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities

short: Possibly vintenar: leader of twenty soldiers.
note: Possibly vintenar, a medieval English officer commanding a vintaine, a unit nominally of twenty soldiers whose actual strength varied.

sources.label: University of Liverpool · study of medieval military levies

short: A religious company in ancient Greece.
note: A company or association gathered for religious celebration in ancient Greece, particularly the singing and dancing associated with Dionysus.

short: An old French battle trumpet.
note: An Old French and Anglo-Norman word for a horn or trumpet used to give signals in battle.

short: An extinct giant soaring bird.
note: Teratornis is a genus of large extinct birds. Teratornis merriami, found at La Brea, resembled a condor and exceeded the California condor in size.

sources.label: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County · La Brea Tar Pits

short: A North African hooded robe.
note: An older form of djellaba, a loose outer robe with a hood, associated especially with North Africa.

short: Adriatic Slavs; Venetian mercenary troops.
note: An old Italian name for the Slavic peoples of the eastern Adriatic, also used for Slav soldiers serving the Republic of Venice.

short: A small auxiliary knife.
note: French bâtardeau: a small knife or dagger carried in the sheath of a larger dagger or sword.

short: Possibly Panthera atrox, the American lion.
note: Possibly Panthera atrox, the extinct American lion, a large Ice Age cat. Latin atrox means fierce or frightful.

sources.label: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County · La Brea Tar Pits

short: An Egyptian term for the shadow.
note: An older Egyptological transcription for a person’s shadow, treated as a constituent of the person in ancient Egyptian religious accounts.

sources.label: E. A. Wallis Budge · introduction to the Book of the Dead

short: Possibly phrontisterion: a place for thought.
note: Possibly Greek phrontisterion, a place for thinking or study; Aristophanes uses the name for Socrates’ school in The Clouds.

short: Possibly the noctule bat; also French for a brief note.
note: Possibly noctule, the common name of Nyctalus noctula, a large bat with long, narrow wings. French notule also means a short note or annotation, from Latin notula, little mark.

short: Darkening or tending toward black.
note: Becoming black, blackish, or approaching black in color; from Latin nigrescere, to grow black.

sources.label: Noah Webster · American Dictionary of the English Language (1828)

short: Latin: a seer, prophet, or poet.
note: Latin vates means a prophet or seer; it also denotes a poet, linking poetry with inspired utterance.

short: Latin: sand or an arena.
note: Latin harena means sand, and also the sand-covered place of combat in an amphitheater, the source of English arena.

short: Latin: a eunuch.
note: A Latin word for a eunuch or, more broadly, someone regarded as incapable of procreation. It also described unfruitful plants.

short: An interpreter of lightning omens.
note: A priest who interpreted omens from lightning in ancient Rome; Latin fulgurator can also mean one who hurls lightning.

short: Latin: a trident.
note: A three-pronged spear or trident, associated with Neptune and used by the net-fighting gladiators called retiarii.

short: Possibly Latin hasta: spear or lance.
note: Possibly Latin hasta, a spear or lance. The word also served as a symbol of military and magisterial authority.

short: A many-headed sea monster of Greek myth.
note: A monster inhabiting the rocks opposite Charybdis. In Homer’s Odyssey she has six heads on long necks and snatches sailors from vessels passing her cave.

short: A visible appearance of a deity.
note: A manifestation in which a god becomes visible. The word comes through Greek theophaneia, combining the divine with the idea of appearing.
